title: Shortcrust Pastry
subtitle: the all-purpose pastry for tarts, pies, and quiches
excerpt: Shortcrust pastry is the foundation of British baking. Cold butter, minimal handling, and a short rest are the three things that determine whether it is crumbly and tender or tough. This version works for both sweet and savoury dishes.
sourceNotes: Classic British shortcrust. The ratio of fat to flour is the standard 1:2.

recipe.yieldDescription: Makes enough for 1 double-crust pie or 2 pastry cases
recipe.freezeNotes: Wrap in cling film and freeze for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch and freeze half for future use.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 3 days ahead. Wrap and refrigerate.
recipe.temperatureNote: Bake blind at 200C for 15 minutes before filling

content.text: Keep everything cold. Cold butter, cold water, cold hands if possible. Warmth develops the gluten and makes the pastry tough. Work quickly and stop as soon as the dough comes together.

items.prepNote: use 2-3 tbsp ice-cold water -- just enough to bring the dough together

content.text: Put the flour, salt, and sugar into a large bowl. Add the cold butter cubes. Rub the butter into the flour with your fingertips until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs with some pea-sized lumps remaining.
Mix the egg yolk with 2 tablespoons of cold water. Add to the flour mixture. Use a knife to cut it in, then bring the dough together with your hands. Add the third tablespoon of water only if needed.
Press the dough into a flat disc. Wrap in cling film. Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes before rolling.
On a lightly floured surface, roll the pastry to about 3mm thickness. Work from the centre outwards and turn the pastry a quarter turn after each roll.
Line the tin by draping the pastry over your rolling pin and lowering it in. Press into the edges without stretching. Chill again for 20 minutes before blind baking or filling.

items.cause: Stretched into the tin rather than pressed in, or not rested before baking.
items.fix: Always drape the pastry loosely into the tin and let it fall into place. Chill before baking.

items.symptom: Pastry is crumbly and falls apart when rolled
items.cause: Not enough liquid, or too cold when rolling.
items.fix: Add water a teaspoon at a time. If too cold, leave at room temperature for 5 minutes before rolling.

content.text: Shortcrust pastry underpins a vast portion of the British baking repertoire -- from savoury quiches and pork pies to treacle tarts, mince pies, and fruit pies. Master this and dozens of other recipes open up. It is one of the most useful things to be able to make by hand.
